evidence_quotes.quote: The implementation of the DP and the TPS controls—makes possible, or obstructs—the laying of trunk infrastructure and the construction of WDSs, which in turn, determines the ability or inability of a neighborhood to legally receive municipal water supply.

Land for building urban infrastructure in Ahmedabad is made available through a two-stage planning process called the development plan (DP)–town planning scheme (TPS) mechanism and is governed by the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act (GTPUD Act), 1976.

But as the authors show in this case, Ahmedabad’s planning authorities are indeed capable of going to quite some lengths to accommodate existing informal constructions (such as changing ratios where allocation of open space is concerned) and make changes to otherwise standard planning norms to map and build basic services.

This essay draws on 24 months of qualitative research in Ahmedabad, between 2016 and 2018. It draws on insights from interviews and dialogues including those with residents, community organizations, NGO oﬃcials, ward councillors (politicians), municipal engineers and bureaucrats, planners, builders, formal and informal business owners, and academics as well as on legal, oﬃcial, and media documents
Second, households that are unable to access municipally supplied water (legally or illegally) resort to drawing water from the ground, from shared or private borewells, if they have the means to.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines neighborhood and household access to piped municipal water supply provided by the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC) in two predominantly Muslim wards (Makhtampura and Sarkhej).
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines urban governance, statutory land-use planning, municipal incorporation, and judicial intervention shaping municipal water supply. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it specifically analyzes statutory land-use, zoning, and tenure/landownership rules under the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act (1976) Development Plan-Town Planning Scheme (DP-TPS) mechanism (where retaining agricultural zoning bars TPS implementation and piped water infrastructure, TPS rules engage only legal landowners rather than informal occupiers or illegal subdivisions, municipal property tax collection is delinked from tenure status, planning authorities exercise regulatory discretion and selective accommodation via overlay zones or modified planning norms, and Gujarat High Court public interest litigation orders enforce municipal water provision) that directly govern whether neighborhoods can legally receive municipal piped water infrastructure and supply.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary qualitative socio-legal empirical evidence based on 24 months of fieldwork in Ahmedabad (2016-2018), including interviews and dialogues with residents, ward councillors, municipal engineers and bureaucrats, planners, NGO officials, builders, landowners, and analysis of development plans, legal cases, and official documents. Qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are eligible for the systematic review mechanism synthesis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports exclusion from and unmapped access to piped municipal water supply (absence of trunk mains and local water distribution stations needed to deliver municipal Narmada water to residences, leaving households reliant on private or shared groundwater borewells).
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (neighborhoods and households in Makhtampura and Sarkhej wards in Ahmedabad, alongside municipal, planning, and landowner actors), exposure (statutory zoning, land-pooling/tenure rules, administrative discretion/accommodation, legal contestations, and judicial directives in the DP-TPS planning process), outcome (legal mapping and provision of trunk mains, water distribution stations, and piped municipal water supply), and study design (qualitative socio-legal / institutional ethnography case study).

study_design: Qualitative socio-legal case study / institutional ethnography (24 months of interviews and document/plan analysis, 2016–2018)
population_and_sample: Neighborhoods and residents of two predominantly Muslim municipal wards in Ahmedabad, India (Makhtampura, estimated >400,000 residents, ~95% Muslim; and Sarkhej, ~50% Muslim), examined via 24 months of qualitative interviews with residents, community organizations, NGO officials, ward councillors, municipal engineers/bureaucrats, planners, builders, landowners, and business owners (unit of analysis: neighborhood/ward and household access)
exposure: Statutory land-use zoning, land-readjustment/tenure rules (landowner-only engagement vs informal/illegal subdivisions), administrative discretion and regulatory accommodation (e.g., rezoning, overlay zones, planning norm exceptions), landowner legal contestations, and High Court enforcement orders under the Development Plan–Town Planning Scheme (DP–TPS) process (Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976)
outcome: Legal mapping, extension of municipal water infrastructure (trunk pipelines and local water distribution stations), and neighborhood/household access to or exclusion from piped municipal water supply
rationale: This empirical qualitative socio-legal case study (24 months of fieldwork in Ahmedabad, 2016–2018) investigates how statutory land-use zoning, landownership/tenure requirements, administrative discretion and selective accommodation, landowner legal contestations, and High Court judicial directives under the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act (1976) Development Plan–Town Planning Scheme (DP–TPS) mechanism directly govern the extension of trunk infrastructure, water distribution stations, and legal access to piped municipal water supply in Makhtampura and Sarkhej wards. It satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, and per review safeguards, qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are included for mechanism synthesis.
